questions.question: Why did separate m. and www. sites break down?
options: Too many devices: tablet, phablet, mini tablet — which site do they get?
questions.explanation: Do you direct a tablet to the mobile website or to the desktop? What about a large phablet phone? An iPad Mini?

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Do you direct a tablet to the mobile website or to the desktop?

questions.question: A better approach is?
options: The same HTML and CSS for all users, rendering differently from viewport size.
questions.explanation: A far better approach is to serve the same HTML and CSS to all your users. By using a few key techniques, you can make your content render differently, based on your user's browser viewport size.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: A far better approach is to serve the same HTML and CSS to all your users.

questions.question: Who popularized the name responsive design here?
options: Keith J. Grant coined it in 2018.
questions.explanation: This approach, popularized by web designer Ethan Marcotte, is called responsive design.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: This approach, popularized by web designer Ethan Marcotte, is called responsive design.

questions.question: Media queries alter the design based on?
questions.explanation: Using media queries to alter your design based on viewport size.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Using media queries to alter your design based on viewport size

questions.question: Mobile first means?
options: Design desktop first, then delete columns.
Design with small-screen constraints first, then enhance for larger screens.
questions.explanation: The mobile first approach dictates you design your site with these constraints in mind from the beginning. Then progressive enhancement for large screen users.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: the mobile first approach dictates you design your site with these constraints in mind from the beginning.

questions.question: Duckett's layout chapter includes?
options: Designing for different sized screens, and fixed vs liquid layouts.
questions.explanation: Discover how various devices have different screen sizes... Learn the difference between fixed width and liquid layouts.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett
reference.excerpt: Discover how various devices have different screen sizes and resolution

questions.question: A hamburger icon in Grant's example is?
options: Three lines that toggle a hidden menu on small screens.
questions.explanation: This icon, with three horizontal lines, is often called a hamburger icon.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: This icon, with three horizontal lines, is often called a hamburger icon

questions.question: Which query is mobile first?
questions.explanation: Base styles are the small screen. min-width adds layout as the viewport grows.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant

questions.question: A forced desktop/mobile split causes?
options: More problems than it solves, plus a second site to maintain.
questions.explanation: A forced dichotomy between desktop and mobile causes more problems than it solves. Plus, you have to maintain an extra website.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: a forced dichotomy between desktop and mobile causes more problems than it solves.

questions.question: Liquid vs fixed, in Duckett's list?
options: Fixed uses a set width; liquid grows with the screen.
questions.explanation: Learn the difference between fixed width and liquid layouts, and how they are created.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett
reference.excerpt: Learn the difference between fixed width and liquid layouts, and how they are created.

questions.question: Where should the mobile menu button live in Grant's markup note?
options: Inside the nav, so one nav serves mobile and desktop.
questions.explanation: The button to toggle the menu for mobile screens is inside the nav element. The nav-menu is placed where it can meet your needs for both mobile and desktop designs.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: the button to toggle the menu for mobile screens is inside the nav element.

questions.question: A mobile layout, in this chapter, is mostly?
options: A no-frills design focused on the content.
questions.explanation: A mobile layout is mostly a no-frills design. Apart from the interactive menu, this design is highly focused on the content.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: A mobile layout is mostly a no-frills design.

questions.question: Which width rule is fluid, not a locked 960px page?
questions.explanation: A percentage width plus a max-width is a liquid box that will not grow past a readable measure.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett

questions.question: If a mobile user needs a desktop-only action, the two-site model fails because?
options: You hid that action on m. and they cannot reach www. without a fight.
questions.explanation: What if a mobile user wants to perform an action you only have available on the desktop version of your site?

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: What if a mobile user wants to perform an action you only have available on the desktop version of your site?

questions.question: Progressive enhancement here means?
options: Get the small layout working, then add large-screen layout in min-width queries.
Require the newest browser or show nothing.
questions.explanation: Once your mobile experience works, you can use progressive enhancement to augment the experience for large screen users.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: you can use “progressive enhancement” to augment the experience for large screen users.
